item.title: “But this body, Aggivessana, is material, composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to…
item.description:
“But this body, Aggivessana, is material, composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to rubbing, pressing, breaking, disintegration, dissolution. It should be contemplated as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as not-self. When he contemplates this body as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease … as not-self, then bodily desire, bodily fondness, bodily subjection are abandoned.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 74 – Dīghanakhasutta

item.title: “‘A being, a being,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is one called a being?” - “Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving…
item.description:
“‘A being, a being,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is one called a being?” - “Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving there is for form — entanglement there, immersion there — thus one is called a being. For feeling … perception … formations … for consciousness — entanglement there, immersion there — thus one is called a being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.2

item.title: Elder Nun Upasanā: Upasanā, cross the strong flood, The flood so hard to cross, Subject to the King of Death. Bear this last body, Having…
item.description:
Elder Nun Upasanā:

Upasanā, cross the strong flood,
The flood so hard to cross,
Subject to the King of Death.
Bear this last body,
Having conquered Māra and his army.

From: Therīgāthā 1.10

item.title: - “Venerable sir, I do not understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One regarding the purpose of purity of virtue.” - “Monk, if you…
item.description:
- “Venerable sir, I do not understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One regarding the purpose of purity of virtue.” - “Monk, if you do not understand the Dhamma I have taught regarding the purpose of purity of virtue, then how, monk, do you understand the Dhamma I have taught?” - “Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One as greed and the removal of greed.” - “Good, good, monk! Good, monk! You understand the Dhamma taught by me as greed and the removal of greed. It is for the purpose of greed and the removal of greed, monk, that the Dhamma is taught by me. What do you think, monk: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?” - “Impermanent, venerable sir.” - “The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … Is the mind permanent or impermanent?” - “Impermanent, venerable sir.” - “What is impermanent — is that suffering or happiness?” - “Suffering, venerable sir.” - “What is impermanent, suffering, subject to change — is it fitting to regard it as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” - “No, venerable sir.” - “Seeing thus, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … disenchanted with the mind … Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.74

item.title: “Monks, I do not see any other hindrance by which beings, hindered, wander and transmigrate for a long time as this hindrance of ignorance. Monks,…
item.description:
“Monks, I do not see any other hindrance by which beings, hindered, wander and transmigrate for a long time as this hindrance of ignorance. Monks, hindered by the hindrance of ignorance, beings wander and transmigrate for a long time.

No other thing so hinders beings,
That they run on by day and night,
As that of delusion’s snare.

But one who has abandoned delusion,
Pierced through the mass of darkness,
No longer wanders on —
In them the cause is no more.”

From: Itivuttaka 14

item.title: “Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and…
item.description:
“Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and humans delight in sound … in odor … in taste … in touch … in phenomena, are excited by phenomena. When phenomena change, fade, and cease, devas and humans dwell in suffering.

Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches,
And all phenomena —
Desirable, delightful, agreeable —
Thus they are called.

Devas and humans in the world,
Regarding them as delightful —
Where they cease and fade away,
Devas and humans see suffering.

The noble one sees as ease
When identity view is destroyed —
The noble one sees as opposite
All the views of the world.

What others call pleasure,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as pleasure.

See the Dhamma, hard to comprehend,
Where the ignorant are bewildered —
Darkness for the blind,
Obscurity for those who cannot see.

The wise are open-eyed,
Like light clearly shining,
The foolish, even though near,
Do not understand the Dhamma.

Overcome by the thirst of birth,
Swept away by the current of existence,
Subject to Māra’s control —
They do not awaken to this Dhamma.

Apart from the noble ones, no one
Awakens to this path —
The path leading to Nibbāna,
With perfect wisdom, free from defilements.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.136

item.title: - What gives birth to a person? What always runs about? What undergoes rebirth? Because of what is there no liberation? - Craving gives birth…
item.description:
- What gives birth to a person?
What always runs about?
What undergoes rebirth?
Because of what is there no liberation?
- Craving gives birth to a person,
The mind itself always runs about,
Beings undergo rebirth,
Because of suffering, there is no liberation.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.56

item.title: Four wheels, nine doors, Full of defilement, tied by greed — Mired in mud, O great hero, What will be the future state Of such…
item.description:
Four wheels, nine doors,
Full of defilement, tied by greed —
Mired in mud,
O great hero,
What will be the future state
Of such a human birth?

(The Blessed One):
Having cut off delight and bondage,
Sensual desire and evil,
Having destroyed the root of craving —
Such will be his future state.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.29

item.title: Elder Sabbhakāma: This two-footed creature, Impure and foul-smelling, Full of various corpses — From it, fluid oozes. With deer, use a trap; with fish, a…
item.description:
Elder Sabbhakāma:

This two-footed creature,
Impure and foul-smelling,
Full of various corpses —
From it, fluid oozes.

With deer, use a trap; with fish, a hook;
With monkeys, a pit;
Thus worldlings are caught.

Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, touches —
Agreeable and pleasing —
These five strands of sensual pleasure
Are known in female form.

Worldlings, with mind infatuated,
Run after enjoying female form.
The terrifying cemetery increases,
Storing up renewed existence.

One who avoids female form
As a foot avoids a snake’s head —
That mindful one overcomes
The world’s poisoner.

Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures,
Security in renunciation,
Having escaped all sensual pleasures,
I have attained the destruction of defilements.

From: Theragāthā 6.14

item.title: “Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple has conscience (hiri): he is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, ashamed of evil, unwholesome states. He has…
item.description:
“Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple has conscience (hiri): he is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, ashamed of evil, unwholesome states. He has fear of wrongdoing (ottappa): he fears bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, fears evil, unwholesome states.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 53 – Sekhasutta
